strengths: Addresses an important and timely topic: investigating whether modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) truly possess 3D visual geometry and spatial understanding capabilities.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper tests 25 representative open-source and proprietary models across a wide spectrum of model sizes (1B to 78B parameters), providing extensive empirical evidence of current MLLM shortcomings in 3D and geometric reasoning.
Detailed documentation: the appendix provides thorough implementation details, including prompt designs, tool specifications, and category breakdowns across diverse datasets.
weaknesses: Limited dataset novelty in SpatialScore: A large portion of SpatialScore (approximately 22K out of the 28K total samples) is an aggregation and repackaging of 11 existing, previously published benchmarks (e.g., CV-Bench, BLINK, MMIU, VSI-Bench, VSR, SpatialSense, QSpatialBench, 3DSRBench). While unified evaluation protocols have utility, assembling existing benchmarks offers limited scientific and technical contribution.

Unnatural and questionable task formulations in VGBench: Several tasks in VGBench involve selecting or predicting floating-point camera intrinsic matrices, homography matrices, or perturbed rotation matrices directly via text QA (e.g., choosing between slightly perturbed 3x3 matrix values). Standard vision-language architectures are token-based autoregressive models, not floating-point numeric regressors; testing whether an MLLM can differentiate slightly perturbed numbers in matrix form conflates arithmetic/numerical discrimination with visual spatial intelligence.

Unfair baseline comparison and limited technical novelty in SpatialAgent: SpatialAgent is a standard Plan-Execute / ReAct tool-use agent built on off-the-shelf vision expert models (SIFT, RAFT, DepthAnythingV2, VGGT, SAM2, OWLv2). In Table 3, comparing SpatialAgent directly against naked MLLMs on tasks like depth and homography estimation is fundamentally unfair, as SpatialAgent delegates the core visual geometric computation directly to specialized tools (e.g., SIFT for homography, DepthAnything for depth). The paper does not benchmark against existing vision agent/tool-use baselines (e.g., Visual ChatGPT, ViperGPT, HuggingGPT).

Incomplete evaluation of SpatialAgent: The performance of SpatialAgent is only reported on the 1.4K SpatialScore-Hard subset in Table 3. Its results are notably absent from the primary benchmark tables for VGBench (Table 1) and full SpatialScore (Table 2), leaving the overall effectiveness and failure modes across the broader benchmark unclear.

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark scale and unification: The paper unifies 11 existing spatial benchmarks with a newly constructed visual geometry benchmark (VGBench) to produce SpatialScore (28K QA pairs), covering single-image, multi-frame, and video modalities across 8 core spatial categories.

Rigorous evaluation of MLLM capabilities: The benchmark is evaluated across an extensive suite of 25 MLLMs ranging from 1B to 78B parameters, including general foundation models, proprietary frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Gemini 2.0 Flash), and spatially fine-tuned models.

Well-curated hard subset (SpatialScore-Hard): The 1.4K hard subset is carefully filtered using consensus failure from multiple models across varying sizes followed by human verification, effectively isolating critical failure modes in 3D perception and visual geometry.

Effective tool-augmented baseline (SpatialAgent): The proposed SpatialAgent incorporates 9 open-source vision and geometry tools (e.g., DepthAnythingV2, VGGT, OrientAnything, RAFT) and benchmarks both Plan-Execute and ReAct paradigms, demonstrating significant improvements over direct model inference on challenging spatial tasks.

High clarity and reproducible implementation details: The paper and appendix provide extensive documentation, including exact prompt templates, tool specifications, category breakdowns, and comprehensive per-dataset results.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty in benchmark composition: Over 78% of SpatialScore (22K out of 28K samples) is aggregated from existing published benchmarks (e.g., RealWorldQA, CV-Bench, BLINK, VSI-Bench, VSR), which makes the primary new data contribution centered on VGBench (6K samples).

Artificial question formats in VGBench: Certain visual geometry tasks—such as matching numerical 3x3 homography matrices, camera intrinsic parameters, or full transformation matrices via multiple choice—are somewhat unnatural for vision-language evaluation and may test numerical text matching rather than genuine visual-spatial reasoning.

Incomplete evaluation of SpatialAgent: While SpatialAgent is shown to be effective on SpatialScore-Hard (Table 3), results for SpatialAgent on the complete SpatialScore and VGBench are omitted in the main tables. It is important to assess whether tool orchestration introduces latency, failure propagation, or regressions on simpler/standard spatial queries.

Limited architectural analysis: The discussion primarily correlates performance with parameter scale and task type, offering limited technical diagnosis into why certain vision encoders or architectural choices (e.g., native dynamic resolution vs. fixed patch grids) succeed or fail on geometric estimation.

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark unification: SpatialScore consolidates 11 existing spatial benchmarks with the newly created VGBench, offering a large-scale (28K samples) and diverse testbed spanning multiple modalities (single image, multi-image, video) and question formats.

Introduction of VGBench: VGBench addresses a clear blind spot in current MLLM evaluations by targeting explicit visual geometry perception tasks (e.g., relative camera pose, homography estimation, point tracking, and metric depth/distance) with precise 3D ground truth.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The paper conducts an impressive evaluation across 25 modern MLLMs ranging from 1B to 78B parameters, as well as proprietary models, clearly demonstrating the severe limitations of current architectures in geometric and 3D spatial reasoning.

Well-documented methodology and reproducibility: The appendix provides extensive details, including exact prompting templates, tool definitions, scoring criteria, and category distributions across datasets.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in SpatialAgent: SpatialAgent is essentially a standard tool-augmented agent pipeline combining off-the-shelf vision models (OWLv2, SAM 2, Depth Anything V2, VGGT, RAFT, SIFT) orchestrated via classic Plan-Execute or ReAct prompting frameworks. While effective as an engineering demonstration, it lacks methodological novelty.

Questionable formulation for certain visual geometry tasks: Asking standard MLLMs to identify or output raw numeric 3x3 homography matrices, camera rotation/translation vectors, or exact pixel/metric parameters often reduces to chance-level guessing (e.g., Table 1 shows homography matrix accuracy hovering around 25%, exactly chance on 4-way multiple-choice questions). It is unclear whether this evaluates spatial understanding or the impossibility of predicting ungrounded floating-point matrices without visual tool assistance.

Incomplete evaluation of SpatialAgent: While SpatialAgent results are reported on the 1.4K SpatialScore-Hard subset in Table 3, its results are not included in the main tables (Table 1 for VGBench and Table 2 for full SpatialScore), making it harder to assess overall performance gains across the full distribution of tasks.

High reliance on dataset aggregation: Aside from the 6K VGBench samples, 22K of the 28K samples in SpatialScore come directly from existing datasets (e.g., VSI-Bench, 3DSRBench, SpatialSense, CV-Bench). While standardizing these under one framework is convenient, the primary original data contribution is limited to VGBench.
